claims.text: Controlled high-temperature exposure activates Mg diffusion out of the metastable solid-solution matrix.
Mg preferentially diffuses toward grain boundaries during thermal exposure.
Accumulation of Mg at grain boundaries triggers the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
The resulting Mg-rich intermetallic compounds are discrete and localized at grain boundaries.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates disrupt the continuity and integrity of the protective oxide or passivation film.
Disruption of the protective film diminishes corrosion resistance.
Disruption of the protective film diminishes high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial metastable solid-solution state has a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial state has an intact, continuous passivation layer and high corrosion resistance.
The initial state has high oxidation resistance.
Exposure at 500–1100 °C in oxygen-rich or corrosive atmospheres represents the relevant high-temperature service regime.
Increasing temperature and exposure time can affect interdiffusion and intermetallic growth kinetics.
An intermetallic nucleation inhibitor can suppress Mg-rich phase formation.
Heat-treated samples will develop pronounced Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries.
Heat-treated samples will show lower corrosion resistance than the initial or nucleation-inhibited samples.
Heat-treated samples will show lower high-temperature oxidation resistance and less-uniform oxide scales.
Nucleation-inhibited samples will largely retain a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
Nucleation-inhibited samples will maintain superior corrosion and oxidation protection.
Reported Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys form intermetallic phases and exhibit measurable corrosion behavior and passivation.
The precise Mg diffusion kinetics and their quantitative relationship to protective-film breakdown remain undetermined.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experimental design describe a comparison between thermally exposed samples with and without a nucleation inhibitor, whereas the falsification rule refers to a comparison between untreated and inhibitor-treated samples. These are not the same controls.
